title: Which model for the help desk?
scenario:
Your IT help desk wants an AI assistant to sort incoming requests (password reset, hardware, software, access) and draft a first reply. About 3,000 requests arrive each day. Staff want replies within a few seconds. The budget is tight.

A vendor salesperson says: "Just use our newest, most powerful model. It tops every benchmark." Your manager asks for your recommendation.

questions.prompt: What is the best way to start?

options.text: Use the most powerful model, because it tops the benchmarks.
options.explanation: Benchmarks are not your task. For a simple, high-volume task with tight speed and budget needs, the strongest model may be slower and cost more than you need.

options.text: Start with a fast, low-cost model, test it on real requests, and move up only if it falls short.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic's guide calls this efficiency-first and says it suits high-volume, simple, cost-sensitive tasks with tight speed needs. That is this help desk.

options.text: Use whichever model a colleague uses for writing reports.
options.explanation: Report writing has different needs. Choose for this task's capability, speed and cost.

options.text: Wait until a better model comes out.
options.explanation: New models keep coming. A tested choice now, with a test set to recheck later, beats waiting.

questions.prompt: How should the team decide whether the chosen model is good enough?

options.explanation: Vendor benchmarks don't use your requests. Anthropic's guide says to test with your actual prompts and data.

options.text: Try three requests and see if they look fine.
options.explanation: Three examples is too few to catch the common mistakes. Use a set of real cases with known good answers.

options.text: Ask the model how accurate it is.
options.explanation: The model's own claim is not a measurement. Only tests on your real requests tell you how it performs.

options.text: Run 20–30 past requests with known correct categories through it, and score the results.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic's guide says a good evaluation set is the most important step, and OpenAI's guide says to compare results on the same inputs.

questions.prompt: The low-cost model sorts requests well, but its draft replies to access problems are often weak. What should you try first?

options.text: Raise the model's effort or reasoning setting for those requests, and test again.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic's guide says tuning effort is often a better lever than switching models. OpenAI's guide also treats the reasoning setting as part of the choice.

options.text: Switch everything to the most expensive model.
options.explanation: Sorting already works. Paying more for every request to fix one category wastes budget. Try a cheaper lever first.
Most of the task already works. Fix the weak part instead.

options.text: Send access requests to the most capable model right away, without testing.
options.explanation: Maybe later. Anthropic's guide says tuning effort is often a better lever than switching models. And without a test set you can't tell whether the switch fixed anything.
